solution:
In every case apply Lenz's law: the induced current flows so as to oppose the change in flux that produces it. Which way round that comes out in letters depends on how each coil is wound, so read the winding in the figure before naming the path.
(a) The magnet approaches south-pole first, so the flux through the coil directed from the coil towards the magnet increases. The face of the solenoid nearer the magnet must become a south pole, so as to repel the approaching south pole. With this coil wound as drawn, the induced current flows along \(qrpq\).
(b) Left circuit: the magnet's south pole approaches, exactly as in (a), so again the face nearer the magnet must become a south pole. This coil is wound the opposite way to the one in (a) — its leads leave the bottom of the former rather than the top — so the same requirement is now met by a current along \(prq\). Right circuit: the magnet's north pole recedes, so the flux through that coil directed away from the magnet decreases. Its face nearer the magnet must become a south pole, so as to attract the receding north pole; the current flows along \(yzx\).
(c) The tapping key has just been closed, so the current in the first coil is rising from zero and the flux it sends through the second coil is increasing. The induced current opposes that increase and flows along \(yzx\).
(d) Changing the rheostat setting changes the current in the driven coil, so the flux through the labelled coil changes and the induced current opposes the change. The driven coil here carries its current in the opposite sense to the one in (c), so the flux threading the labelled coil points the other way and the induced current is reversed: it flows along \(zyx\).
(e) The tapping key has just been released, so the current in the first coil is dying away and the flux it sends through the second coil is falling. The induced current flows so as to maintain that flux, i.e. in the same sense as the decaying current: along \(xry\).
(f) No current is induced. The field lines of the straight current-carrying wire are circles concentric with the wire, and they lie entirely in the plane of the loop. The flux linked with the loop is therefore zero at every instant, so however fast the current falls there is no change of flux and no induced emf.
_note: First draft had (a) as qprq and (d) as yzx; both were inverted by a misreading of the drawn winding sense, and were corrected against the printed key. The physical statements (which face becomes which pole, and (f)) were correct throughout and are unchanged. Recorded as OUR-ANSWER-WRONG in the crosscheck.

solution:
[Textbook misprint in the answer key: it gives the induced-current path as "Along adcd", which visits \(d\) twice and never reaches \(b\) — that is not a closed loop and cannot be a current path. The intended string is \(adcb\), which is the answer below and is what the key's own parenthetical requires (the flux increases, so the induced current must oppose it). Only the letter string is broken; the direction and the reasoning printed alongside it are correct.] (a) The field is directed into the plane of the paper. For a wire of fixed length the circle encloses the greatest area, so as the irregular loop turns into a circle its area increases and the inward flux through it increases. By Lenz's law the induced current must set up flux out of the plane of the paper inside the loop, so it flows anticlockwise, i.e. along \(adcba\).
(b) The field is directed out of the plane of the paper. As the circular loop is deformed into a narrow straight wire the area it encloses falls almost to zero, so the outward flux through it decreases. The induced current must set up flux out of the plane of the paper to oppose the decrease, so it again flows anticlockwise, i.e. along \(a'd'c'b'a'\).
In both cases the induced current opposes the change in area that is causing the flux to change.
_note: The sense (anticlockwise in both cases) is fixed by the field direction printed in Fig. 6.16 and by the change in enclosed area; the lettered path additionally assumes the labels run b (left), c (top), d (right), a (bottom) as drawn.

solution:
The loop lies inside the solenoid with its plane normal to the axis, so it is linked by the solenoid's field \(B = \mu_0 n I\).
Number of turns per unit length, \(n = 15\,\text{turns cm}^{-1} = 1500\,\text{turns m}^{-1}\).
Area of the loop, \(A = 2.0\,\text{cm}^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2\).
Rate of change of current, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{4.0 - 2.0}{0.1} = 20\,\text{A s}^{-1}\).
The induced emf is
\(\varepsilon = A\dfrac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mu_0 n A \dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}\)
\(= (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 1500 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-4}) \times 20\)
\(= 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{V}\)
Induced emf \(= 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{V} = 7.5\,\mu\text{V}\), lasting only while the current is changing.

The loop has a cut, so no current flows and the emf across the cut is the motional emf \(\varepsilon = Blv\), where \(l\) is the length of the side that cuts the field lines. Here \(B = 0.3\,\text{T}\) and \(v = 1\,\text{cm s}^{-1} = 1 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The emf lasts only while the loop is leaving the field region, i.e. for the time taken to travel the length of the other side.
(a) Motion normal to the longer side: the side cutting the field is \(l = 8\,\text{cm} = 8 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\).
\(\varepsilon = 0.3 \times (8 \times 10^{-2}) \times (1 \times 10^{-2}) = 2.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{V}\)
The loop must move through its \(2\,\text{cm}\) width, so \(t = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{1 \times 10^{-2}} = 2\,\text{s}\).
(b) Motion normal to the shorter side: \(l = 2\,\text{cm} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\).
\(\varepsilon = 0.3 \times (2 \times 10^{-2}) \times (1 \times 10^{-2}) = 6 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{V}\)
The loop must move through its \(8\,\text{cm}\) length, so \(t = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{-2}}{1 \times 10^{-2}} = 8\,\text{s}\).
(a) \(2.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{V}\), lasting \(2\,\text{s}\).
(b) \(6 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{V}\), lasting \(8\,\text{s}\).

Each element \(\mathrm{d}r\) of the rod at a distance \(r\) from the axis moves with speed \(v = \omega r\) at right angles to the field, so it contributes \(\mathrm{d}\varepsilon = Bv\,\mathrm{d}r = B\omega r\,\mathrm{d}r\). Integrating from the axis to the ring,
\(\varepsilon = \displaystyle\int_0^L B\omega r\,\mathrm{d}r = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega L^2\)
With \(B = 0.5\,\text{T}\), \(\omega = 400\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\) and \(L = 1.0\,\text{m}\),
\(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 400 \times (1.0)^2 = 100\,\text{V}\)
Emf between the centre and the ring \(= 100\,\text{V}\).

The wire falls at right angles to the horizontal component of the earth's field, so the motional emf is \(\varepsilon = B_H l v\).
(a) \(\varepsilon = (0.30 \times 10^{-4}) \times 10 \times 5.0 = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{V}\)
(b) Take east, north and vertically upward as a right-handed set. The horizontal component of the earth's field points north and the velocity is vertically downward, so the magnetic force per unit charge on a positive carrier, \(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\), points east. The emf therefore drives conventional current from the western end to the eastern end inside the wire, that is, from west to east.
(c) Positive charge accumulates at the eastern end, so the eastern end is at the higher electrical potential.
(a) \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{V} = 1.5\,\text{mV}\).
(b) From west to east within the wire.
(c) The eastern end.

The magnitude of the average self-induced emf is \(|\varepsilon| = L\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\).
Here \(\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}\right| = \dfrac{5.0 - 0.0}{0.1} = 50\,\text{A s}^{-1}\) and \(|\varepsilon| = 200\,\text{V}\), so
\(L = \dfrac{|\varepsilon|}{|\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t|} = \dfrac{200}{50} = 4\,\text{H}\)
Self-inductance of the circuit \(= 4\,\text{H}\).

The flux linkage with the second coil produced by a current \(I\) in the first is \(N\Phi = MI\), so the change in flux linkage is
\(\Delta(N\Phi) = M\,\Delta I\)
\(= 1.5 \times (20 - 0) = 30\,\text{Wb}\)
Change of flux linkage with the other coil \(= 30\,\text{Wb}\).
